title: Feedback, errors, undo, and honest progress
outcome: Design visible system state and recovery for slow, failed, and partially completed work.
useCase: Exports, bulk changes, uploads, and background jobs.
benefits: Builds accurate expectations and supports recovery.
drawbacks: Honest progress needs observable backend states, not only frontend animation.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Name the real state. Keep a recovery path.

trace.title: Action acknowledged
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

After an action, people need to know whether the system heard them, whether work is still running, and what changed.

“Saved” means something different from “Queued.” A progress indicator must describe the boundary it actually observes.

Use a determinate bar only when you know a meaningful total. Use a clear waiting state otherwise.

Approximate response-time heuristics can help thinking, but no single threshold fits every network and task. Tell people what they can safely do while waiting.

Prevent predictable errors where possible. For reversible actions, an understandable Undo can be less disruptive than repeated confirmation dialogs.

For irreversible or high-consequence actions, make the target and consequence explicit. A confirm dialog that says only “Are you sure?” adds interruption without understanding.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Trace click → acknowledged request → accepted job → processing → result or failure. Map each message to a real backend state.

An optimistic UI should explain pending state when the result is not yet confirmed.

For partial success, show successful and failed items separately with a retry policy. Do not make users reconstruct a 50-item selection from memory.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
A spinner with no timeout/recovery can feel abandoned. A percentage based only on elapsed time can be misleading.

Toasts that vanish before users read them are poor error storage.
